Meet hardware can join Teams calls, while Android-based Microsoft Teams Rooms can join Google Meet meetings. Google started addressing that problem last month when it previewed a new interoperability feature that would let Meet and Teams hardware work together. title: A strange YouTube login bug is locking some users out of the website
summary: Reports suggest an account-specific sign-in bug could be affecting multiple browsers.
body: TL;DR Some YouTube users can’t sign in on web browsers, even though their Google accounts work normally elsewhere. Reports span multiple browsers and computers, with affected accounts still working in the YouTube mobile and TV apps. The issue has been escalated for investigation, but Google hasn’t publicly explained what’s causing it or when a fix may arrive. YouTube only recently put out one login fire after fixing a bug that locked some viewers out on TVs and gaming consoles . But while that problem was getting attention, another sign-in headache appears to have been quietly frustrating a much smaller group of YouTube users on the web. Reports stretching back roughly two weeks describe accounts that work normally across other Google services but refuse to sign in to YouTube in a browser. A Reddit user said clearing cookies, switching browsers, using Incognito mode, changing passwords, and even trying another computer made no difference. Their affected accounts still worked in YouTube’s mobile app.

title: Gemini Live’s camera just became much more useful for accessibility
summary: Gemini can now describe your surroundings and guide your camera with spoken cues.
body: TL;DR Google is rolling out Guided Vision in Gemini Live for blind and low-vision users. Gemini can describe what the camera sees and verbally guide users to reframe the shot when needed. Guided Vision works on Android 9 and newer in markets that support Gemini Live. For blind and low-vision users, pointing a phone camera at something is only useful if the phone can explain what it sees. Google has been building towards just that with Gemini Live for more than a year, first adding visual guidance that could highlight objects on-screen . And now the company is turning that idea into a more accessibility-focused tool called Guided Vision. Guided Vision is rolling out today in Gemini Live on compatible Android phones. Once enabled, users can share their camera and hear real-time descriptions of what’s around them, ask follow-up questions, and get spoken instructions to adjust the camera. If Gemini needs a better view, for example, it can ask you to pan right, tilt down, or step back.

body: TL;DR Attackers created a fake ChatGPT model called “Plus 5.6” on the real ChatGPT website. It sent users to a fake security check that tricked them into running a malicious Windows command. That command could install malware that could access files, the screen, the webcam, the microphone, and more. There was a time when spotting a sketchy download meant looking for misspelled websites, strange pop-ups, and other obvious red flags . But that gets much harder when the scam starts on a website you already trust. Security researchers have uncovered a malware campaign that does exactly that, using a real ChatGPT page to convince people they’re dealing with an official OpenAI product before redirecting them to a far more dangerous site. Researchers at Huntress (via TechRadar ) found attackers abusing ChatGPT’s Custom GPT feature to create a bot called “Plus 5.6.” The name was chosen to sound like an official OpenAI model, and because Custom GPTs are hosted on ChatGPT.com, anyone opening the link would see a legitimate ChatGPT address in their browser.

Pages support text, images, charts, files, comments, and help from ChatGPT, Codex, or Dots. It’s rolling out to Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, with Slides and Sheets coming later. ChatGPT has gotten pretty good at helping you make something, but finishing the job often means taking that work somewhere else. You brainstorm in ChatGPT, paste the result into a document, invite your coworkers, collect feedback, then return to the chatbot for another round. OpenAI now wants to cut out that shuffle with ChatGPT Space, a new shared workspace where people and AI can keep working on the same material together. Space, announced at OpenAI’s DevDay alongside the new GPT-6.1 Sol model and its always-on Dots agents , replaces Library for eligible users. It acts as a home for pages, uploaded files, folders, and eventually presentations and spreadsheets, while Projects continue to exist separately for chats, files, and project instructions.

title: I planned my entire vacation with Claude, and I’m never going back
summary: I used Claude to organize a three-week Japan trip, turning my research and preferences into a flexible itinerary.
body: I’m not a big fan of LLMs as decision-making tools, but they do serve a purpose in my workflow as an organization layer. Specifically, when it comes to travel. The problem is that if you ask Gemini , ChatGPT, or Claude to plan a multi-day trip to Tokyo, you will probably get a generic list of tourist attractions. It might tell you to visit Tsukiji market at noon, suggest a restaurant that closed two years ago, and send you across the city three times in one afternoon. That tracks, since it’s just basing its recommendations on the collective knowledge of the internet — both old and new. AI doesn’t really know your preferences, how much walking you can handle, or whether visiting a particular spot actually makes sense given everything else on your itinerary. title: Claude maker warns that advanced AI could be a ‘catastrophic’ threat to humanity
summary: Anthropic’s darkest AI warnings are now part of its pitch to investors.
body: TL;DR Anthropic’s IPO filing warns that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” The company says models have exhibited behaviors such as resisting shutdown, hiding information, and engaging in actions resembling blackmail. The warning formalizes concerns Anthropic researchers and other AI leaders have already raised publicly. The AI industry has no shortage of people warning that the technology they’re building could eventually become dangerously hard to control . Researchers and executives across Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and other labs have raised concerns ranging from runaway autonomy to human extinction. Until now, though, those warnings have mostly lived in interviews, research papers, and lengthy essays. But Anthropic appears to be taking them somewhere new: Wall Street. Reuters reports that the Claude maker’s IPO prospectus warns investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” which is quite the risk disclosure from a company preparing to sell investors on the enormous upside of that same technology.
